thread.title: Got a new smartphone for Christmas? Here’s what you need to know about device protection plans

author: kopitiambot.com
title: Got a new smartphone for Christmas? Here’s what you need to know about device protection plans
text:
(Source: marketwatch.com )
It was a typical Wednesday morning. I was making my way out of my apartment building and walking to the train when I tripped over my shoelace and dropped my iPhone.
Yes, my still-in-great condition iPhone 6S I had gotten as a gift for Christmas the year prior. And as my luck would have it that morning, my phone seemingly landed on the only pebble on the sidewalk in front of me, instantly shattering my screen.
But because I had invested $159 of my own money in a three-year cell phone protection plan from SquareTrade — one of several third-party insurance providers — this simple mishap didn’t become a budget-buster. Rather, I paid a $25 deductible and took advantage of SquareTrade Go, the company’s on-demand device repair service. That afternoon, a technician met me at my office, and I was able to watch as he replaced my smartphone’s screen on the spot.
I’m far from alone, of course. Americans have rung up quite the bill fixing their cracked smartphone screens. A recent study from SquareTrade , which is a subsidiary of Allstate
ALL, +0.28%
found that American smartphone owners broke more than 50 million screens in the past year and spent $3.4 billion to fix them. That same report estimated that two-thirds of smartphone owners had damaged their phone in some way.
And as the price tag for mobile devices has increased, so has the cost to repair them. The iPhone Xs Max costs $1,099 if purchased through a single payment with Apple
AAPL, +0.05%
. Replacing the device’s screen, meanwhile, would cost $329 without insurance, which is double the average price for a new screen.
Also see: Gifts to help people unplug and get back to a life before smartphones
Moreover, the iPhone Xs and other top-end smartphones now feature entirely-glass casing and more advanced facial recognition technology embedded within the phone. That’s raised the cost of non-screen repairs to as much as $599. For context, that’s what a brand-new 8 gigabyte model of the original iPhone cost when it was first released. “Electronics are getting more expensive and more breakable,” said Jason Siciliano, global creative director and vice president at SquareTrade.
While that’s arguably made smartphone insurance a more worth-while investment, purchasing a protection plan is not a fool-proof decision. Here is what consumers should consider:
Who is using the smartphone — and what device did they receive When it comes to choosing the right smartphone protection plan, the biggest consideration should be that person’s habits, experts said. “Are they accident-prone? Do they have small children?” said Kelsey Sheehy, personal finance expert at Nerdwallet. “If yes, then insurance would be a thoughtful add-on.”
A survey from Consumer Reports found that 81% of people with young children who had a smartphone had lost at least one device in the past two years.
Another consideration is the device in question. If it’s one of the flagship models from Apple or Samsung
SSNLF, -3.07%
, an insurance or protection plan can make sense due to the sheer cost of the device itself. However, for consumers who purchase a low-end smartphone, insurance may not make as much sense, said Chris Raymond, deputy editor at Consumer Reports.
What plans are out there and how much do they cost There are essentially three types of smartphone insurance or protection plans: Warranty plans offered by manufacturers such as Apple or Samsung, warranty and protection plans offered by mobile carriers such as AT&T
T, +1.10%
or Verizon
VZ, +0.22%
and third-party plans from companies like SquareTrade. The plans offered by wireless carriers are typically administered by other insurance companies, such as Asurion and Assurant
AIZ, +0.27%
From a cost perspective, some plans will charge users on a monthly basis (though they can cancel at any time), while with other plans consumers can pay in full upfront for a certain length of coverage. Wireless phone protection from mobile carriers can start as low as $3 a month — that’s the cost of the Wireless Phone Protection plan from Verizon — and increases in cost based on the amount of coverage a consumer receives or the type of device covered. These plans are usually charged on a monthly basis.
Third-party insurers such as SquareTrade and Geek Squad, from Best Buy,
BBY, -1.19%
have plans that begin at $8.99 a month and increase in cost depending on the device. Comparatively, manufacturers like Apple and Samsung charge a single flat rate for protection coverage for a set period of time, roughly between $99 and $269, depending on the coverage and device.
All insurance plans come with deductibles that must be paid before repairs are covered. These can be as low as $19 and as high as $250, depending again on the model.
To judge the value of an insurance plan, Raymond suggested that consumers compare the cost of un-insured repairs with the cost of the plan itself. “That would give you a pretty good idea that the insurance is worth it,” he said.
Read more: Can Apple make an iPhone that isn’t bad for the environment?
What plans do and don’t cover Accidental damage and out-of-warranty malfunctions are typically covered by insurance plans. Like any insurance plan, consumers will need to file claims and have them approved by their insurer to receive compensation.
Many providers, including mobile carrier plans from Asurion and SquareTrade, offer same-day services for simple repairs such as replacing a screen in most major cities for as little as $25.
But sometimes plans have limitations even on what they typically cover. For instance, some plans will only cover two or three instances of accidental damage in a given year. Other plans, including SquareTrade, also limit the number of times a smartphone user can replace their device’s battery. Intentional damage to a device is not covered typically.
And when it comes to replacing a device beyond repair, plans’ courses of action vary. Some will provide money to be used for the purchase of a new device, while others will provide a replacement device. In the latter case, replacement devices are often refurbished models — and not always the same model that the consumer originally owned.
Another area where smartphone protection plans vary widely in coverage is theft and loss of the device. SquareTrade, for instance, never covers these events — Siciliano said this was because theft and loss are much rarer than accidental damage but cost more, so SquareTrade foregoes that coverage to keep the cost of its plans down. Some plans, such as AppleCare and Geek Squad Protection, charge more for consumers who want theft and loss protection. With other companies, including AT&T, this protection comes standard.
Some plans may also require consumers to get their devices fixed by a specific company — and it’s not always the original manufacturer. That’s in part why Philip Michaels, senior editor at electronics review website Tom’s Guide, gravitates toward manufacturers’ plans. “I feel better about handing my stuff over to Apple to look at,” Michaels said. “AppleCare is pretty generous with its terms, even if one might argue it’s a little pricy.”
Don’t miss: How your iPhone could save your life
Consider alternatives to smartphone insurance There are other ways to cover a lost or damaged smartphone beyond paying for a special insurance policy. If you received a smartphone as a gift and pay for your monthly phone bill with certain credit cards — including the U.S. Bank Visa Platinum Card
USB, -0.15%
the Wells Fargo
WFC, +0.55%
Propel American Express Card
AXP, -0.27%
and the Deserve Pro Mastercard
MA, -1.34%
— cell phone insurance may be included.
Consumers’ devices may also be covered under their homeowner’s or renters insurance plans — or they can speak with their insurance agent to add additional coverage .
Some people, including consumer spending expert and radio host Clark Howard , are against smartphone insurance plans, arguing that the costs can easily stack up and the exclusions can prevent them from being useful. Instead, he and others suggest purchasing a sturdy case, which can prevent against most forms of accidental damage. “That’s a small $30 outlay that will save you a lot of heartache,” Michaels said.
